1.pericope_label: The call to come up, the graded approach, and the people's consent to all the words of the Lord

schools.summary: Explain the missing subject of the opening verb as a seam, the Book of the Covenant having been inserted at this point as an originally distinct document, so that this verse once followed directly on the notice that Moses drew near unto the thick darkness; identify Nadab and Abihu as Aaron's two elder sons and deny that these seventy are the judges appointed earlier, who did not yet exist, making them instead the heads of tribes and families who had held authority in Egypt. Elsewhere restrict the phrase all the words of Jehovah, which cannot mean the decalogue since the people heard that directly from God, to the words about altars that follow it, and take all the rights for the chapters of judgments — holding that the recital and the people's answer were not yet the covenant but the preparation for it, since they had to know what was imposed and promised and to declare themselves willing before it could be made.

Raise the difficulty that the seventy are elsewhere not chosen until after Sinai yet appear here before the Law is promulgated, and resolve it by supposing that each tribe had already appointed six governors of its own, making up the number, so that when the lawgiver was later relieved of his burdens the government was transferred to men already honourably distinguished, an established custom being hard to depart from; add the conjecture that the number commemorated the seventy who went down into Egypt with Jacob; explain that the Tables had to be fetched before the tabernacle was consecrated, since an ark with nothing in it would leave the sanctuary in a manner empty, and that the train of companions was to rouse their minds for the blessing; count three gradations in the approach — the people worshipping afar off, the elders and priests admitted closer as witnesses, and the mediator alone received into the higher glory; and insist that the verbs are imperative and not past, since what is reported is not yet what was done but what God commanded. Ask also who it was that spoke, and answer that it was no doubt a divine Person.

Report the complaint that the events are out of order, and the repair that rearranges them, so that God laid all the laws before Moses on the mount and told him that once the people had ratified the conditions they were to come up again with Aaron's sons and the elders; give the arrangement as topography, the people at the foot, Aaron with his sons and the elders perhaps half way up, and Moses alone to the summit; note that the people had heard the voice less distinctly than Moses, like the hoarse grumbling sound of distant thunder; and draw the devotional lesson that before they came near they must worship, so that we must enter God's gates with humble and solemn adorations, the mediator being a type of Christ who as high priest entered alone into the most holy place.

Teach that before coming near they must worship, so that we enter God's gates with humble and solemn adorations, drawing near as those who know their distance — and press it with the question whether, when great princes are approached with the profound reverences of the body, the soul that draws near to God should not be bowed before him; make the mediator a type of Christ entering alone into the most holy place; observe that when a communion is begun between God and us it shall never fail on his side if it do not first fail on ours; hold that the people were told all the precepts, general and particular, of the foregoing chapters, and were not led blindfold into the covenant nor taught a devotion that was the daughter of ignorance; and turn their unanimous consent into a lament, that people will not always stay in the good mind they sometimes seem to be in.

debates: Why the opening verse has no stated subject.
Whether the seventy elders here are the same body chosen later, and how the two accounts agree.
How far each party was permitted to ascend.
What all the words of the Lord covers, and whether the recital was itself the covenant.
outliers: Ellicott explains the disorder as a literary insertion; Clarke reports a rearrangement of the events instead.
Calvin alone supplies a pre-Sinai body of six governors per tribe to reconcile the two accounts of the seventy.
Clarke alone describes what the people heard as the grumbling of distant thunder.
Keil alone excludes the decalogue from the words recited, on the ground that the people had already heard it directly.
Wesley's two notes in these verses are abridgements of Henry's at the same verses.

3.pericope_label: The people told all the words of the Lord, the book written, the altar and twelve pillars, and the sacrifices

schools.summary: Take the recital to include the ten commandments as well as the laws and ordinances of the preceding chapters; hold that God probably taught the mediator the use of letters there on the mount, and that he taught them to Israel, from whom they afterwards travelled to Greece and the other nations, adding that as soon as God separated a peculiar people to himself he governed them by a written word, as he has ever since and will while the world stands; describe the altar as probably of turf, as commanded, with twelve unhewn stones set round about it, the altar representing the throne of God and the stones the tribes, these being the two parties entering into covenant, and guess that each tribe set up and knew its own pillar with its elders standing by; and take the young men for stout, able and reputable men chosen from the tribes for killing, flaying and offering, noting which victims belonged to burnt offerings and which to peace offerings.

Exclude the ten commandments from the recital, since the people had heard them from the Lord themselves, and confine it to the judicial laws of the two preceding chapters, setting aside the rabbinic list of Noachide commands, sabbath, honouring parents and the red heifer as either already known or not yet given; distinguish likewise what was written from the ten commands, which the Lord wrote himself; decline the view that the young men were the firstborn serving as priests before Aaron, the objections not being easily refuted, and take them for choice young men separated for the service without regard to birthright, as the elders were chosen from the graver sort; give the twelve stones a different office from the other commentators, namely that they stood by the altar so the people might know they were not kept at a distance in token of rejection but only that, conscious of their unworthiness, they might humble themselves, being still remembered before God, who embraced them by means of these monuments — which bore no human shape, being heaps of stones and not images; and set the sacrifice in a wider frame, that covenants have in every age and among the heathen been accompanied with sacrifice, the division of the blood between altar and basins being the symbol by which this covenant was ratified through its mediator and surety.

Take the recital as an outline, the general purport and main heads but probably not the details, since otherwise there would have been no need to read the book to them afterwards, and observe that the people gave their adhesion willingly, feeling the laws to be holy, just and good and not yet knowing how hard perfect obedience would prove; note that the mediator's familiarity with writing is presumed throughout the Pentateuch, one learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians being unlikely to lack so ordinary an Egyptian accomplishment; identify the hill and describe the pillars as long stones set on end, symbolising the tribes as the altar symbolised Jehovah; deny that the young men were firstborn officiating by primogeniture or sons of Aaron, making them servants of the mediator, who performed the sprinkling himself; supply the principle that even under the Levitical priesthood any Israelite might slaughter the victim and lay the flesh on the altar, only the sprinkling and the kindling being reserved to the priest; and distinguish burnt offerings, at once expiatory and signs of self-dedication, from peace offerings, which express gratitude, the two together marking thankfulness for the covenant and resolve to be wholly consecrated.

debates: Whether the recital included the ten commandments, and whether it was full or an outline.
Whether Moses already knew how to write, or was taught letters on the mount.
What the twelve pillars signified — a contracting party, or a pledge that the distanced people were remembered.
Who the young men were, and why they and not priests performed the sacrifice.
outliers: Ellicott alone notes that the people consented before they knew how hard obedience would be.
Wesley derives the alphabet from Sinai by way of Israel to Greece; Ellicott treats writing as an ordinary Egyptian skill Moses already possessed.
Calvin alone reads the pillars as consolation for the people's distance rather than as the second party to a contract.
Gill and Keil independently reject the theory that the young men were firstborn acting as priests.
Ellicott alone states which sacrificial acts were reserved to priests and which were not.

6.pericope_label: The blood divided, the book of the covenant read, and the people sprinkled

schools.summary: Explain why the halving is unusual — the sprinkling on the altar was the most essential act of every sacrifice, by which the victim as representative of the offerer was delivered up to God, and ordinarily all the blood was so devoted, only here being needed for another purpose; distinguish the verb used of the half thrown on the altar, which is swung from the vessel, from the sprinkling done afterwards, and note that several young oxen yielded blood enough for many to be caught by it; take the two halves to have reference to the two parties, brought by the covenant into a living unity, while disputing among yourselves whether the rite has anything to do with the blood-communion customs common throughout the East, one denying any connection whatever and the other citing Homer, Herodotus, Xenophon, Lucian and Tacitus to show that such usages were felt to add force and sacredness to an agreement; identify the book as the collection written overnight, from the altar-law after the decalogue to the end of the promises; deny that the blood was sprinkled on the twelve pillars, since the words scarcely admit it and the Epistle to the Hebrews understood the people to be sprinkled, allowing only that it fell on their representatives; and take the consecration as the qualification for the ascent that follows, made not by the whole nation, which was impracticable, but by its representatives, Aaron's sons being summoned with reference to their future priesthood.

Leave open whether the remainder was sprinkled on the people themselves or on the pillars that represented them; expound the two sprinklings, the blood on the altar being the blood of what the people offered and signifying their dedication of themselves, so that all Israel was presented as living sacrifices, and the blood on the people being the blood of a sacrifice God had owned and accepted, signifying his conferring his favour and all its fruits from a God reconciled to them; read the words spoken over it as a seal both ways, God sealing to be a God to them and they to be a people to him, the promises on both sides being yea and amen; carry it forward to the Mediator of the new covenant, of whom this mediator was a type, who having offered himself on the cross sprinkled his blood on the altar in his intercession and sprinkles it on his church by word and ordinances and by the Spirit of promise; and note that no covenant was reckoned ratified until a sacrifice had been offered, the two sprinklings showing both sides bound — God to support, defend and save, the people to fear, love and serve him — so that the blood of the new covenant was needed to propitiate the throne of justice on the one hand and reconcile men to God on the other.

Note that the basins were set by for the people; and draw attention to what is easily missed, that the book was not only law but contained God's promises to send his angel before them, to drive out the Canaanites and to put them in possession, so that there were promises on both sides — a restipulation of parties, which is what made it a formal covenant.

debates: Why only half the blood went on the altar, when ordinarily all of it did.
Whether the rite has anything in common with the blood-covenants of the heathen.
What the book of the covenant contained, and whether it was law only.
Whether the blood was sprinkled on the people or on the pillars that represented them.
outliers: Keil denies any connection with heathen blood-covenants; Ellicott documents them from six classical authors.
Keil alone distinguishes the verb for swinging blood from the vessel from the verb for sprinkling.
Gill alone insists the book was bilateral, containing promises as well as laws.
Ellicott alone appeals to the Epistle to the Hebrews to settle who was sprinkled.
Keil alone explains the summoning of Aaron's sons as a preparation for their future priesthood.

9.pericope_label: The elders go up, see the God of Israel, and eat and drink before him

schools.summary: Explain why the chapter does not end at the sprinkling: by the ordinary ideas of the time the ratification was complete, but a sacrifice implied a sacrificial meal, and the summons of the first verse meant it was to be held on the mountain — a meal always being an act done before God and involving communion with him, which God signalised by making his presence not merely felt but seen, not amid thunders and darkness but in his loveliness, so impressing on them the mild relation into which a covenant not yet infringed had brought them; hold that the appearance was probably in human form, as the prophets saw him, and deny that the later declaration about seeing no similitude refers to this occasion, since the appearance had feet; identify the stone as probably lapis lazuli and the last phrase as the very heaven itself; and read the concurrence of seeing God and eating and drinking as a forecast of the Christian's highest privilege, the presence of God realised in the Holy Communion. Elsewhere note that the representatives left the mountain with the mediator when the meal was over, though it is not expressly said.

Say that they had some glimpse of his glory in light and fire but saw no manner of similitude, his being one whom no man hath seen nor can see, and that the Greek has them see the place where the God of Israel stood, something that came near a similitude and was not; observe that nothing is described but the pavement, since our conceptions of God are all below him and fall infinitely short, so that they saw not so much as his feet but only a splendid work as of sapphires, the heavens themselves being the pavement of God's palace; and turn it into a comparison, that wisdom was from eternity God's delight and lay in his bosom while the sapphires are only the pavement under his feet — there let us put all the wealth of this world, and not in our hearts.

Insist that the sight was not a vision of prophecy nor with the eyes of the understanding but corporeal, and that what they saw was the Son of God in human form, a pledge and presage of his incarnation, rejecting the Targum's restriction of the sight to two of the company and its hint that their looking was criminal, since this was a privilege; set aside the reading by which the hand not laid on them means a prophetic gift withheld, calling that exposition a violent distortion, and connect the clauses instead — although they saw God, his hand was not laid on them, but they ate and drank; ground the wonder in the ancient proverb that no man shall see God's face and live, and in the patriarch's astonishment at his own preservation, since if the mountains melt at the sight of him what must happen to a mortal; and give the reason it went otherwise here, that they had not rashly thrust themselves forward but come at God's call — whence our boldness never exceeds its bounds nor can be charged with presumption when founded on God's command, while worse than any self-confidence is the timidity that under pretence of modesty distrusts his word.

Hold that the elders were chosen as representatives to witness the manifestation, so that the certainty of the revelation was established by many witnesses of the most competent kind; take the pavement literally and mineralogically as inlaid work of the kind the Romans left behind them, and argue that sapphire is not necessarily blue, ruby and topaz being of the same genus, so the pavement may have been of many colours with the whole body of heaven shining on it, adding the conjecture that the Israelites below saw it over their heads; report and reject the reading that makes the hand withheld a gift of prophecy; note that God was generally apprehended never to show his glory in this manner except to manifest his justice, which is why their survival struck them; and add that the splendour was moderated and they were strengthened to bear it, so that they kept not only their lives but their vigour, courage and comfort, the vision casting no damp on their joy but increasing it, since it is of the Lord's mercies we are not consumed.

debates: Why a further scene was needed once the covenant had been ratified.
Whether they saw a form, or only light and fire without similitude.
What the sapphire pavement was, and whether the people below saw it too.
What it means that God did not lay his hand upon the nobles.
What the eating and drinking in God's presence signified.
outliers: Gill and Ellicott, from different schools, both read the appearance as the Son in human form; Henry and Wesley deny any similitude was seen.
Henry alone weighs the sapphire pavement against wisdom and turns it into a warning about wealth.
Clarke alone treats the pavement as mineralogy and conjectures that the people saw it overhead.
Gill, Clarke and Calvin independently report and reject the same reading, that the withheld hand means a withheld prophetic gift.
Calvin alone draws from the elders' safety a rule about boldness, that what rests on God's command is never presumption, and that timidity is worse than self-confidence.
Ellicott alone names the Holy Communion as what the covenant meal forecasts.

12.pericope_label: Moses called higher to receive the tables, Joshua taken with him, and Aaron and Hur left in charge

schools.summary: Turn the command to be there into a rule, that those who would have communion with God must not only come to ordinances but abide by them, blessed being they that dwell in his house and not they that merely call there; note that the mediator taught nothing but what he had received and received nothing but what he taught, neither adding nor diminishing; explain why his minister was taken up, namely that he might be honoured before the people so they would afterwards take him more readily for their governor, and be prepared for service by training in communion with God, and follow the divine whose observation makes him a type of Christ, since without Jesus, in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, there is no looking into the secrets of heaven; and call the two deputies lords-justices, observing that the people were not left as sheep having no shepherd even for a few days, since good princes find their government a constant care and their people find it a constant blessing.

Reconstruct the interval, the company having gone down into the plain and possibly spent some time there before a second summons came for the mediator and his minister only; notice that neither here nor later are the tables expressly said to have contained the ten commandments, though it is stated plainly elsewhere, and observe that this precludes the fiction of a double decalogue; date the minister's standing from this verse, since his earlier command in battle might have shown no more than military capacity while from here he is plainly the most trusted assistant and so the successor; report the order that the elders remain where they were until the return, with the two deputies appointed to administer justice to whoever had matters of dispute, and make the injunction stricter still, that here means the plain below and the camp was not to be moved however long the colloquy lasted; identify one deputy as the father of Bezaleel and perhaps the mediator's brother-in-law; and say only that we are not told whether the minister followed him into the cloud, a later chapter showing that he was on the mountain though he would not have entered the immediate presence of God.

Deny that the law and commandment promised are any new instruction, the phrase standing in apposition to the tables and explaining them, so that what was given was the authentic writing of the Law already delivered — a divine monument of the covenant, a summary of doctrine written not with ink nor by the hand of man but by the secret power of the Spirit — and decline, with evident reluctance, the speculation of a father you usually defer to about the writing by the finger of God, as more subtle than correct; refuse to take the command to tarry so precisely as to mean one spot, since the adverb indicates our earthly dwelling-place and the elders were plainly sent back to occupy their charge, which they could not do unless in communication with the people; doubt whether the mediator knew how long he would be gone, thinking it more probable he was in doubt and suspense; and end on the six days of fire, conspicuous to all from the least to the greatest, so that none could afterwards pretend not to know from what Author the Law proceeded. Ask also whether the minister fasted the whole forty days, and answer that there is no necessity to suppose it, since the manna fell round about the mountain and he might gather and eat day by day.

Place the company about midway up, there being several stations on the mountain; have the glory above the cloud, so that the mediator left his minister in the cloud and ascended to the glory alone, with frequent conferences between them during the forty days; call the two deputies regents constituted for the absence, since many cases might arise requiring the chief magistrate; and hold that the elders did not tarry the whole time but, after waiting considerably, returned to the camp — their return being supposed the grand cause of the golden calf, since they probably reported that the mediator was lost.

debates: What the command to be there implies about the length of the stay.
Whether the tables promised contained the ten commandments, and whether the law and commandment are anything new.
How far up the mountain the minister went, and how he was fed there.
Whether the elders stayed in the plain or returned to the camp, and what followed.
outliers: Ellicott alone notes that the tables are nowhere here said to hold the decalogue, and uses the silence against a double decalogue.
Calvin declines an interpretation of Augustine's as more subtle than correct.
Gill alone asks how the minister ate during the forty days, and answers from the manna.
Clarke alone makes the elders' return from the mountain the cause of the golden calf.
Wesley reproduces Henry's whole passage on the minister in short, at the following key.

15.pericope_label: The cloud on the mountain six days, the glory like devouring fire, and the forty days

schools.summary: Point out that the article matters, this being the cloud that had accompanied them since Succoth; explain the delay by observing that the mediator would not enter without a positive summons, which it pleased God to put off six days, doubtless spent in the prayer and meditation that fitted him for near contact with Deity; state that the forty days include the six of waiting and passed without eating or drinking, and hold the number itself significant, since it recurs at the second stay, in the prophet's journey to Horeb in the strength of the angel's food, and in the fasting of Jesus at his temptation; report that to the Israelites in the plain a light like a conflagration rested on the summit the whole time; and close the door on modern imitations of such a fast as in all probability impostures.

Read the covering as a lesson, a visible token of God's special presence, since he so shows himself to us as at the same time to conceal himself, letting us know enough to assure us of his power and grace while intimating that we cannot find him out to perfection; reckon that the ascent was on the first day of the week so that the seventh, on which God spoke, was the sabbath; deny that the six days belong to the forty, reasoning that the minister was with the mediator through them and ate of the manna and drank of the brook, so that the mediator probably ate and drank with him, and that only when he was called into the midst of the cloud, leaving the minister outside to go on eating daily, did the fast begin; call the entry into the cloud an extraordinary presence of mind furnished by grace, without which he durst not have ventured; hold that the appearance was calculated to inspire the deepest reverence and godly fear, our God being a consuming fire, and that the people, seeing that fire and finding him long delayed, probably supposed he had been devoured by it and so fell the more easily into idolatry; explain the fast by saying that body and soul alike were so sustained by the invigorating presence of God that he needed no earthly support, which may be the simple reason why he took none; and close with a fourfold reflection — that he alone was permitted to draw nigh and was therein a type of Christ, who alone has access for the human race; that the law can inspire nothing but terror apart from its sacrifices, and those nothing except as they refer to the Lamb of God; and that the blood sprinkled on altar and people together showed that the death of Christ gave Divine justice what it demanded and men what they needed.

Insist that it was not devouring fire but only like it — so large a body of light, so clear and bright, that it looked like flames consuming all in their way, and being on the top visible at a great distance throughout the camp; think it probable that the six days are to be counted within the forty, since the text does not say he was in the cloud forty days; say that the mediator must at that moment have been endowed with more than ordinary courage, the glory flashing out of the cloud like flames, yet being called he was not intimidated but went in with composure; and note the order of the clause, that he went into the cloud after ascending the summit and not before, which the English wording might mislead a careless reader about.

debates: Which cloud is meant, and why the summons was delayed six days.
Whether the six days of waiting are counted within the forty.
Whether the appearance on the summit was fire or only like fire.
How the fast was sustained, and what the whole transaction typifies.
outliers: Ellicott alone gives the six days' delay a devotional purpose.
Wesley alone argues from the minister's eating that the fast began only at the entry into the cloud.
Clarke offers a second and different cause for the golden calf here, having given another a few verses earlier.
Ellicott alone dismisses modern imitations of the forty-day fast as probable impostures.
Clarke alone closes with a fourfold summary of the chapter's typology.
